answer:
**Text-to-speech must decide both what sounds to produce and how to realize them as a waveform.** A traditional neural pipeline predicts acoustic features such as a mel spectrogram, then a vocoder synthesizes samples. Duration modeling determines how long phonemes last; prosody controls rhythm, emphasis, and pitch. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04558) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.06103)

FastSpeech-style systems use explicit duration information to generate many acoustic frames in parallel. VITS combines different ingredients, including latent-variable modeling, flows, and adversarial waveform synthesis; it should not be treated as merely another identical mel-plus-vocoder pipeline.

Codec language models generate discrete audio codes that a codec decoder turns into sound. This makes audio generation resemble sequence modeling over a learned vocabulary. Flow-matching systems instead learn a velocity field that transports noise toward a speech representation, then integrate that field during synthesis. These categories can overlap in how representations are encoded and decoded.

**Compare the whole listening experience.** A system can have a good average real-time factor yet delay the first audible chunk. Another can start quickly but mishandle long text, punctuation, or rare names. Measure intelligibility, natural prosody, speaker similarity where relevant, first-audio delay, and sustained generation speed. Count iterative refinement and vocoder cost rather than assuming fewer autoregressive tokens automatically means lower latency. Speaker-conditioned generation should use appropriate consent and speaker controls.

**Technical details and references.**

Acoustic-model pipelines predict features such as mel spectrograms, then synthesize waveform with a vocoder. FastSpeech-style duration modeling enables parallel generation; VITS combines variational modeling, flows, and adversarial waveform generation, so it is not simply the same architecture. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04558) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.06103)

Codec language models generate discrete audio-code sequences and decode them to waveform; some use autoregression, others masked parallel refinement. Flow-matching TTS learns a conditional velocity field and integrates from noise to speech representations. These categories can overlap.

Compare intelligibility, prosody, speaker similarity, first-audio latency, real-time factor, and robustness to long or unusual text. Fewer autoregressive steps do not guarantee lower end-to-end latency if iterative refinement or vocoding is expensive. Evaluate consent and intended speaker controls when using voice-conditioning data.
